rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After praise, the worshipers' confession of exclusive worship and help bridges praise to petition; trusting God's welcome and hoping for His favor, they ask for guidance.
rows.anchor: فكان ذلك واسطة بين الثناء وبين الطلب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The petition is the purpose of the preface, like the subject of a speech or the transition in a poem, fitting the Fātiḥa as a preamble to a book sent as guidance and mercy.
rows.anchor: فهذا هو التوجيه المناسب لكون الفاتحة بمنزلة الديباجة للكتاب الذي أنزل هدى للناس ورحمة

rows.speaker: صاحب الكشاف
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī treats the petition as an answer to an unstated question; Ibn ʿĀshūr prefers to read it as the natural aim of the preceding praise and confession.
rows.anchor: على ما ذهب إليه صاحب « الكشاف »

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The petition is separated from the preceding clauses because those clauses are declarative while this one is imperative.
rows.anchor: ولاختلاف الجمل المتقدمة معها بالخبرية والإنشائية فصلت هذه عنهن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Guidance is gentle direction, especially direction toward what benefits its recipient; its gentleness suits someone for whom good is intended.
rows.anchor: والهداية الدلالة بتلطف ولذلك خصت بالدلالة لما فيه خير المدلول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hadā takes one direct object because its sense resembles irshād, and takes the person guided as a second object through ilā or lām.
rows.anchor: يتعدى إلى مفعول واحد بنفسه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prepositional constructions mean bringing someone to knowledge or guiding them for a purpose; Qur'anic examples use both ilā and li-.
rows.anchor: على معنى أوصلته إلى معرفته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An explanation says direct-object use for the second object is a Hijazi idiom, while other dialects require a preposition; another analysis calls it ellipsis and connection.
rows.anchor: قيل هي لغة أهل الحجاز وأما غيرهم فلا يعديه بنفسه وقد جعلوا تعديته بنفسه من التوسع المعبر عنه بالحذف والإيصال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An unnamed view distinguishes direct-object use for someone already on the path from prepositional use for someone not yet travelling it.
rows.anchor: وقيل الفرق بين المتعدي وغيره أن المتعدي يستعمل في الهداية لمن كان في الطريق ونحوه ليزداد هدى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He rejects that distinction as, at most, a prevalent usage rather than proof that the verb changes meaning with its construction; both huda and hidaya are verbal nouns, while the source noun is hady.
rows.anchor: والحق أن هذا إن تم فهو أغلبي على أنه تخصيص من الاستعمال فلا يقتضي كون الفعل مختلف المعنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hadā necessarily takes one object; for a second, it is direct when it means showing or clarifying, and prepositional when it means general guidance or pointing, so construction signals the embedded sense.
rows.anchor: فالحق أنه إن اعتبر فيه معنى الإراءة والإبانة تعدى بنفسه وإن اعتبر فيه مطلق الإرشاد والإشارة فهو متعد بالحرف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The basic sense is showing someone the route to a destination; guidance meanings developed as widely used metaphors from this literal sense.
rows.anchor: حقيقة الهداية الدلالة على الطريق للوصول إلى المكان المقصود فالهادي هو العارف بالطرق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The migration report says Abū Bakr hired a skilled route guide from Banū al-Dayl, illustrating the literal Arabic sense of hādī.
rows.anchor: إن أبا بكر استأجر رجلاً من بني الديل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In religious usage when ascribed to God, guidance is direction toward deeds pleasing to Him; its opposite, misguidance, is leading someone astray.
rows.anchor: والهداية في اصطلاح الشرع حين تسند إلى الله تعالى هي الدلالة على ما يرضي الله من فعل الخير ويقابلها الضلالة

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority, including the Ashʿarites, define guidance as showing the way to an end whether or not arrival occurs; Ibn ʿĀshūr calls this correct.
rows.anchor: فالجمهور على عدم اعتباره وأنها الدلالة على طريق الوصول

rows.speaker: جماعة منهم الزمخشري
rows.claim: A group including al-Zamakhsharī requires successful delivery in the definition, lest guidance fail to differ from misguidance; their dispute reflects different accounts of divine command and will versus creation.
rows.anchor: وذهب جماعة منهم الزمخشري إلى أن الهداية هي الدلالة مع الإيصال وإلا لما امتازت عن الضلالة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: There is no dispute that guidance culminating in arrival is what religiously should be sought from both guide and guided, though a guide may err or the recipient may reject it.
rows.anchor: ولا خلاف في أن الهداية مع الوصول هي المطلوبة شرعاً من الهادي والمهدي

rows.speaker: عبد الحكيم
rows.claim: ʿAbd al-Ḥakīm chooses a shared sense covering both outcomes because the Qur'an uses guidance for each; absent contrary evidence, neither homonymy nor metaphor is assumed.
rows.anchor: وهذا معنى ما اختار عبد الحكيم أنها موضوعة في الشرع لقدر المشترك لورودها في القرآن في كل منهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Guidance comprises four ordered kinds: innate powers for human existence, rational proofs distinguishing truth, revealed messengers and books for harder matters, and disclosure of higher truths.
rows.anchor: والهداية أنواع تندرج كثرتها تحت أربعة أجناس مترتبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first kind gives sensory and motor powers, from an infant's instinctive feeding and responses to danger through practical needs and the rational power that derives unknowns from knowns.
rows.anchor: الأول إعطاء القوى المحركة والمدركة التي بها يكون الاهتداء إلى انتظام وجود ذات الإنسان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The second kind is theoretical knowledge supplied by proofs that distinguish truth from falsehood and correctness from error.
rows.anchor: نصب الأدلة الفارقة بين الحق والباطل والصواب والخطأ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The third kind comes through messengers, revealed books, and measures of justice for matters beyond proof or too burdensome to settle by proof, as in God's description of the messengers.
rows.anchor: الثالث الهداية إلى ما قد تقصر عنه الأدلة أو يفضي إعمالها في مثله إلى مشقة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The highest kind unveils higher realities and meanings beyond the reach of rational minds through revelation, sound inspiration, or divine manifestations.
rows.anchor: الرابع أقصى أجناس الهداية وهي كشف الحقائق العليا وإظهار أسرار المعاني التي حارت فيها ألباب العقلاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: What a particular supplicant seeks depends on that person's or group's condition; as a prayer taught to all Quran-addressed believers, it requests kinds of guidance distributed according to each person's capacity.
rows.anchor: ولا شك أن المطلوب بقوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some guidance is sought for acquisition by those who lack it, while guidance already possessed, including much of the innate first kind, is sought for its continuance.
rows.anchor: فبعض أنواع الهداية مطلوب حصوله لمن لم يبلغ إليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A request form ordinarily asks that an act or abstention occur; asking only for continuance is figurative, as in the address to believers in 4:136.
rows.anchor: وصيغة الطلب موضوعة لطلب حصول الماهية المطلوبة من فعل أو كف فإذا استعملت في طلب الدوام كان استعمالها مجازاً

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asking for more guidance remains literal when some levels are attained and others lack; seeking increase also entails asking that existing guidance endure, making the request a kināya for continuance as well.
rows.anchor: وأما إذا استعملت في طلب الدوام للزيادة مما حصل بعضه ولم يحصل بعضه فهي مستعملة في معناها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For the Prophet, who had reached guidance's highest degree, the wording is figurative and an appropriation of the verse; the verse itself asks for complete guidance through further attainment and continuance.
rows.anchor: ويكون دعاؤه ذلك اقتباساً من الآية وليس عين المراد من الآية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṣirāṭ means a road; Arabic dialects pronounce it with ṣād or sīn, while the Hijaz dialect uses ṣād, an emphatic substitution easing the transition into emphatic ṭā.
rows.anchor: والصراط الطريق وهو بالصاد وبالسين وقد قرىء بهما في المشهورة

rows.speaker: الجعبري
rows.claim: Al-Jaʿbarī says Arabs change sīn to ṣād before several consonants; here ṣād matches ṭā in emphasis and elevation, avoiding a difficult movement from low articulation to high.
rows.anchor: عن الجعبري إنهم يفعلون ذلك في كل سين بعدها غين أو خاء أو قاف أو طاء

rows.speaker: حمزة
rows.claim: Qays pronounces an intermediate sound between sīn and ṣād, called ishām, which Ḥamza reads in the transmission of Khalaf; al-Qurṭubī reports a pure zāy dialect among ʿUdhra, Kalb, and Banū al-Qayn, but says it is weak and unread.
rows.anchor: وقيس قلبوا السين بين الصاد والزاي وهو إشمام وقرأ به حمزة في رواية خلف عنه

rows.speaker: ابن كثير في رواية قنبل
rows.claim: Most canonical readers use the eloquent ṣād form, while Ibn Kathīr in Qunbul's transmission reads sīn; Ibn ʿĀshūr prefers ṣād for its conformity to the muṣḥaf spelling and the eloquent dialect.
rows.anchor: جمهور القراء وقرأ بالسين ابن كثير في رواية قنبل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Companions wrote ṣād to mark the more eloquent form in Quraysh usage; readers of sīn understood the written form as allowing known dialectal alternation, so the difference concerns pronunciation, not the word's lexical substance.
rows.anchor: فالذين قرأوا بالسين تأولوا أن الصحابة لم يتركوا لغة السين للعلم بها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The spelling of al-muṣayṭir with ṣād likewise preserves a form whose origin is sīn, illustrating how the written ṣād need not rule out sīn pronunciation.
rows.anchor: كما كتبوا المصيطر بالصاد مع العلم بأن أصله السين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-ṣirāṭ is an Arabic word, although al-Naqqāsh and Ibn al-Jawzī report it as the Roman word for road; Abū Ḥātim is also cited, and al-Suyūṭī consequently listed it among loanwords.
rows.anchor: عن النقاش وابن الجوزي أنه الطريق بلغة الروم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The road is a metaphor for truth, through which a person reaches the success of God's approval that Islam seeks.
rows.anchor: والصراط في هذه الآية مستعار لمعنى الحق الذي يبلغ به مدركه إلى الفوز برضاء الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mustaqīm is the active participle of istiqāma, the result of making something straight; it means having no bend or detour.
rows.anchor: والمستقيم اسم فاعل استقام مطاوع قومته فاستقام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A straight road is best because it reaches the destination most directly, without leading its traveller astray, causing hesitation, or producing confusion.
rows.anchor: وأحسن الطرق الذي يكون مستقيماً وهو الجادة لأنه باستقامته يكون أقرب إلى المكان المقصود

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: By metaphor, the straight path is clear truth unmixed with false suspicion, like a road without branching side tracks.
rows.anchor: والمستقيم هنا مستعار للحق البين الذي لا تخلطه شبهة باطل فهو كالطريق الذي لا تتخلله بنيات

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās explains the straight path as the true religion and is also reported to call it the religion of Islam; Ibn ʿĀshūr says the two glosses explain one another.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس أن الصراط المستقيم دين الحق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās's gloss does not mean asking for an obsolete religion: all divinely revealed religions were straight paths for their own communities, as Satan's words about God's path also show.
rows.anchor: ولا يريد أنهم لقنوا الدعاء بطلب الهداية إلى دين مضى وإن كانت الأديان الإلهية كلها صرطاً مستقيمة بحسب أحوال أممها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The definite article evokes a mentally understood kind, requested through its unique instance: straightness is singular, while misguidance has many forms.
rows.anchor: لأنهم سألوا الهداية لهذا الجنس في ضمن فرد وهو الفرد المنحصر فيه الاستقامة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One possible reading takes the path as Islam: God taught this prayer to display His favor, having guided them through earlier Qur'an and continuing to guide through later Qur'an and Prophetic instruction.
rows.anchor: وقد يوجه هذا التفسير بحصول الهداية إلى الإسلام فعلمهم الله هذا الدعاء لإظهار منته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur'an explicitly identifies a straight path as the upright religion to which God guided the Prophet.
rows.anchor: قل إنني هداني ربي إلى صراط مستقيم ديناً قيماً

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He prefers that the path mean all sound knowledge, beliefs, and deeds: enabling people to recognize truth and distinguish it from error according to their capacities, without deviation or religious doubts.
rows.anchor: والأظهر عندي أن المراد بالصراط المستقيم المعارف الصالحات كلها من اعتقاد وعمل بأن يوفقهم إلى الحق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This reading is preferable because people need guidance in every affair, including preserving existing goodness from deficiency or deviation; guidance to Islam continues through its revealed and inferred laws, not only initial acceptance.
rows.anchor: وهذا أولى ليكون الدعاء طلب تحصيل ما ليس بحاصل وقت الطلب وإن المرء بحاجة إلى هذه الهداية في جميع شؤونه كلها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The comprehensive reading makes the transition to the following request, for the path excluding those under anger or astray, apt to the context.
rows.anchor: غير المغضوب عليهم ولا الضالين
